## Solution

We determine all values of $p$ for which
$$\rho(x,y)=\int_a^b|x(t)-y(t)|^p\,dt$$
is a metric on $C[a,b]$. We claim $\rho$ is a metric **if and only if $0<p\le 1$**.

---

### Necessity: $p>0$

For $p<0$: taking $x=y$ gives $|x(t)-x(t)|^p=0^p=+\infty$, so $\rho(x,x)=+\infty\ne 0$. The identity-of-indiscernibles axiom fails.

For $p=0$: $|x(t)-x(t)|^0=0^0$, which is undefined (or, under the convention $0^0=1$, gives $\rho(x,x)=b-a\ne 0$). Either way the axiom $\rho(x,x)=0$ fails.

Hence a necessary condition is $p>0$.

### Sufficiency of the metric axioms for $0<p\le 1$

**(i) Non-negativity and identity of indiscernibles.** For $p>0$, the integrand $|x(t)-y(t)|^p\ge 0$, so $\rho(x,y)\ge 0$. If $x=y$ then $\rho(x,y)=0$. Conversely, if $\rho(x,y)=0$, then the continuous non-negative function $|x(t)-y(t)|^p$ has zero integral, hence is identically zero, so $x(t)=y(t)$ for all $t\in[a,b]$.

**(ii) Symmetry.** $\rho(x,y)=\rho(y,x)$ is immediate from $|x-y|=|y-x|$.

**(iii) Triangle inequality.** We use the key analytic fact: for $0<p\le 1$, the map $\varphi(u)=u^p$ on $[0,\infty)$ is concave with $\varphi(0)=0$, and therefore **subadditive**:
$$(a+b)^p\le a^p+b^p,\qquad a,b\ge 0.$$
(Proof of subadditivity: if $b=0$ it is trivial; if $b>0$, set $r=a/b\ge 0$. Concavity with $\varphi(0)=0$ gives $\varphi(r+1)\le \varphi(r)+\varphi(1)$, i.e. $(r+1)^p\le r^p+1$; multiplying by $b^p$ yields $(a+b)^p\le a^p+b^p$.)

Applying this pointwise with $a=|x(t)-y(t)|$ and $b=|y(t)-z(t)|$:
$$|x(t)-z(t)|^p\le\bigl(|x(t)-y(t)|+|y(t)-z(t)|\bigr)^p\le |x(t)-y(t)|^p+|y(t)-z(t)|^p.$$
Integrating over $[a,b]$ gives
$$\rho(x,z)\le \rho(x,y)+\rho(y,z).$$

Thus all three metric axioms hold for $0<p\le 1$.

### Necessity: $p\le 1$ (failure of triangle inequality for $p>1$)

Suppose $p>1$. Take $[a,b]=[0,1]$ and the constant (hence continuous) functions
$$x(t)\equiv 0,\qquad y(t)\equiv 1,\qquad z(t)\equiv 2.$$
Then
$$\rho(x,z)=\int_0^1|0-2|^p\,dt=2^p,\qquad \rho(x,y)+\rho(y,z)=\int_0^1 1^p\,dt+\int_0^1 1^p\,dt=2.$$
The triangle inequality would require $2^p\le 2$, i.e. $p\le 1$, which contradicts $p>1$. Hence $\rho$ is **not** a metric for $p>1$.

---

### Conclusion

Combining all parts: $\rho(x,y)=\int_a^b|x(t)-y(t)|^p\,dt$ is a metric on $C[a,b]$ if and only if

$$\boxed{0<p\le 1}.$$
